projectDesc.p: The digital part of the SNSF project 'Caroline Spurgeon: Chaucer Allusions, Shakespeare's Imagery, and the Digital Humanities' aims to create the first open-access database dedicated to the criticism and reception of Chaucer throughout history. It draws on the compilation and cataloguing work carried out by Professor Caroline Spurgeon (1869–1942) and collected in 'Five Hundred Years of Chaucer Criticism and Allusion'. This work consists of three volumes and a supplement, which will be systematically transcribed, corrected, enriched, encoded and published online, in order to facilitate future research and bring new perspectives to light.

editorialDecl.p: The original spelling and punctuation are retained. Meaningful layouts are reproduced, i.e. verses, printed marginalia, dots lines, tables, etc. However, we do not consider, the line breaks for prose, the columns or the curly brackets. The same rules apply for special characters and glyphs. Otiose letters are normalised, as well as spaces before punctuation marks.

ab.seg: The manuscripts of the Most Honourable the Marquis of Bath, at Longleat, Co. Wilts. . . . [p. 181] A 4to volume, vellum, 15th century . . . [containing with other non-Chaucerian pieces, The Parsones Tales]. This, in the Table, is called the three parties of Penance. . . [p. 188] Folio, paper, 16th century.—The Temple of Glasse, by Chaucer. Folio, vellum, c. 1400. The Sege of Thebes; by John Lydgate. The Knight's Tale; by Chaucer. Grisild; by Chaucer. Ipomedar. Small folio, paper, 15th century. The outside leaves of each quire are vellum. This volume contains minor poems [p. 189] of Lydgate and Chaucer. Sixteen leaves are wanting, containing, as appears by the table of contents, the Flower and the leaf,1 and part of the Complaint of Mars, of which only the last 32 stanzas are here. The Declaration of deth of pite. . . The assemble of ladyes. The complaint of Annelada against Arcile [sic], the fals Theban Knight (43 stanzas) ... The assemble of foules. The ye and the hert ... The chorle and the birde— Envoy ot 8, beginning, "Go little quayer." Folio, paper, 15th century.—The Temple of Glasse. [p. 198] 1709, May 28. Oxford. Thomas Hearne to Lord Oxford: concerning Chaucer. [See above, 1709, Hearne. The letter was to John Bagford, not Lord Oxford. Oxford sub- sequently acquired Bagford's collections.] 1 [Footnote] Mr. Furnivall says that no manuscript of this poem is known to exist.
